subject: Banking
title: Quantitative Easing Explained
description: Learn Quantitative Easing Explained in one minute.

hook.text: When rates hit zero, central banks can't cut further. So they invented QE: buying bonds to pump money into markets.

buildup.text: The Fed buys government bonds from banks. Banks get cash. The idea is they'll lend it out and stimulate the economy.

discovery.text: QE lowered long-term interest rates and boosted asset prices.

twist.text: QE primarily helped asset owners. If you owned stocks or property, you got richer.

climax.text: QE saved the economy but widened inequality. The rich got richer because they owned the assets that QE inflated.

punchline.text: Rates hit zero. QE pumped trillions into markets. Asset owners won most.

quiz.question: What is quantitative easing?
options: Central banks buying bonds to inject money into the economy

details.summary: Quantitative easing is a central bank tool where the institution buys massive amounts of bonds to lower long-term interest rates and inject liquidity into the financial system when short-term rates are already near zero.
details.whyItMatters: QE became the dominant crisis tool after 2008 and again in 2020. Understanding it is essential because it reshaped financial markets, inflated asset prices, and created trillions in central bank balance sheets.
takeaways: The Fed's balance sheet grew from $900 billion to over $9 trillion through QE
QE lowers long-term rates by removing bonds from the market
Unwinding QE, called quantitative tightening, is equally consequential

faq.question: How is QE different from regular interest rate policy?
faq.answer: Regular policy adjusts the overnight borrowing rate between banks. QE directly purchases longer-term securities like 10-year Treasury bonds and mortgage-backed securities, targeting the rates that affect actual borrowing costs for businesses and consumers.

faq.question: Why is unwinding QE so difficult?
faq.answer: Selling trillions in bonds floods the market, pushing prices down and yields up. Rising yields tighten financial conditions and can destabilize markets. Central banks must unwind slowly and telegraph their intentions carefully to avoid disruption.
